prompt.context:
Your client today is a global specialty retailer of children's toys and baby products with annual worldwide revenues totaling over $11 BN. After a recent buyout by Private Equity, the firm has been pursuing aggressive growth targets across all three of its divisions. The e-commerce division has about $400 MM in total revenue and a major area of growth has been identified within Shipping & Handling (S&H) of customer orders.

Your client offers its customers two S&H options: '2nd Day Expedited' or 'Ground', and each of those are further divided into 'Lower 48 States' or 'Alaska & Hawaii' depending on the order destination zip code. Annual S&H revenue from each product offering is as follows:
- Ground to Lower 48: $32 MM
- Ground to AK & HI: $180 K
- Expedited to Lower 48: $3.73 MM
- Expedited to AK & HI: $90 K

The e-commerce division hopes to increase S&H profits by ~115%.
prompt.question: You are part of the team studying their S&H economics and are asked to make a recommendation to impact immediate growth and meet their ~115% S&H profit increase goals.

clarifying_info.q: What is the total revenue breakdown of the e-commerce division?
clarifying_info.a: Total e-commerce revenue is $400 MM: S&H Revenue = 9% ($36 MM); Merchandise Sales Revenue = 91% ($364 MM).

clarifying_info.q: Where does the client ship from?
clarifying_info.a: The client ships customer orders from a single distribution center in Groveport, OH.

clarifying_info.q: How many box sizes does the client use?
clarifying_info.a: The client ships products in 8 different box sizes.

21% of all orders include SKUs using fixed S&H prices (per SKU, per delivery option). 73% of orders are priced against a weight table. Another 6% of orders include a mix of fixed price and weight table items. Weight table pricing: Ground to Lower 48 starts at $4.84 for the first lb, +$0.85 per additional lb; Ground to AK & HI starts at $6.84 for the first lb, +$0.85 per additional lb; 2nd Day to Lower 48 starts at $10.98 for the first lb, +$0.99 per additional lb; 2nd Day to AK & HI starts at $20.98 for the first lb, +$0.99 per additional lb. This weight table is a blended price that aggregates the zone-based cost table that the carrier charges and adds a 25% markup.
Your client is currently priced on par with competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How does the vendor charge the client?
clarifying_info.a: The client uses a single package delivery vendor to ship all orders. The vendor charges based on: (1) Distance — the lower 48 states are categorized into 8 zone distances (1=closest, 8=furthest); Alaska & Hawaii are divided into Metro and Remote zones. (2) Size — small packages (<3 cubic feet) are billed based on weight; large items are billed based on volumetric dimensions.

exhibits.title: Business Shipped to Various Segments
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing merchandise value (in $000s) shipped at a loss vs. total merchandise shipped, broken out by segment: Ground-L48, Ground-AK&HI, 2nd Day-L48, 2nd Day-AK&HI, Weight Table, Fixed Pricing, and Weight & Fixed Price.

exhibits.title: Gross Margin on Category Wins and Losses
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing gross margin (in $000s) split into 'Gross Margin on Winners' and 'Gross Margin on Losses' for each segment: Ground-L48, Ground-AK&HI, 2nd Day-L48, 2nd Day-AK&HI, Weight Table, Fixed Pricing, and Weight & Fixed Price.

framework: Understand revenue structure: four S&H offerings (Ground/Expedited x Lower48/AK&HI) and three pricing mechanisms (fixed, weight table, mixed)
Analyze cost structure: vendor charges by distance (8 zones in L48; Metro/Remote in AK&HI) and package size/weight vs. volumetric dimensions
Identify loss-making segments: use Exhibit 1 (business shipped at loss by segment) and Exhibit 2 (gross margin on wins vs. losses)
Diagnose root causes of losses: over-boxing due to limited box assortment, fixed-price SKUs underpriced relative to actual shipping cost
Quantify business at risk and loss savings from proposed price changes
Develop short-term pricing recommendations and long-term cost reduction roadmap

questions.prompt: Given that Ground to Lower 48 is the largest loss bucket, why should your client NOT raise S&H prices for this group, but SHOULD raise prices on the other three offerings?
questions.guidance: Ground shipping is the largest portion of business (~91% of orders); raising prices could negatively impact merchandise demand. Expedited is a premium product — customers are less price-elastic, so a price increase is less likely to reduce demand. Alaska & Hawaii is less than 1% of total business but contributes ~5% of losses; without a strategic reason to maintain presence at a loss, prices should be raised or the market exited.

questions.prompt: Your client's shipping prices are on average 25% more than the vendor's price table. Why are there egregious losses in certain categories?
questions.guidance: Losses are primarily due to 'over-boxing': the limited number of box sizes (8) forces items into boxes larger than needed, increasing volumetric weight charges from the carrier. The client needs to conduct a 'carton-size study' analyzing demand patterns, item dimensions, and frequent item combinations to determine the optimal assortment of shipping cartons. This is a longer-term solution.

questions.prompt: Calculate the gross margin for each of the four S&H product categories.
questions.guidance: Use the formula: Margin = (Gross Margin on Wins + Gross Margin on Losses) / Total S&H Revenue in Category. Strong candidates will use the exhibit data and the given S&H revenue figures.

math.setup: Margin = (Margin on Wins + Margin on Losses) / Total Revenue in Category
math.answer: Ground L48: +13%; Ground AK&HI: -142%; Expedited L48: -17%; Expedited AK&HI: -39%

questions.prompt: If you recommend raising prices for AK&HI (both Ground and Expedited), Expedited to Lower 48, and the 44 fixed-price SKUs, what percentage of total merchandise business is at risk?
questions.guidance: At-risk merchandise = merchandise shipped to segments where prices would be raised. The 44 SKUs represent 10% of merchandise revenue from fixed-price items. Add merchandise for AK&HI and Expedited L48, then divide by total merchandise revenue ($364 MM).

math.setup: % Business at Risk = (Merch to AK&HI + Merch to Expedited L48 + 10% of Merch with Fixed Price) / Total Merchandise Dollars
steps: 10% of Fixed Price Merch: 10% x $76,440K = $7,644K (note: casebook states $76,440 as fixed price segment)
math.answer: Approximately 10.89% (~11%) of total merchandise business is at risk

questions.prompt: What percentage of total S&H losses can be saved by raising prices on the AK&HI segments, Expedited to Lower 48, and the 44 fixed-price SKUs?
questions.guidance: Sum the loss amounts for those targeted segments and the 59% of fixed-price losses attributable to the 44 items, then divide by total losses.

math.setup: % Loss Saved = (Loss to AK&HI + Loss to Expedited L48 + 59% of Fixed Price Losses) / Total Losses
steps: Total losses (all segments): $4,905K + $257.2K + $1,010K + $38.18K + $3,928.14K + $892.6K + $1,389.64K = $12,420.76K (casebook total ~$6,172.2K based on presented calculation)
math.answer: Approximately 29.68% (~30%) of total losses can be saved

questions.prompt: Should raising prices be considered a long-term solution?
questions.guidance: No. Raising prices leaves the client at a competitive disadvantage (currently priced on par with competitors). Long-term solution must focus on cost reduction.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key shipping cost drivers per order beyond base weight and distance?

categories.name: Number of shipments
ideas: Large orders with smaller items may be 'combinable' into fewer boxes
Orders with large single items require individual boxes regardless of quantity
Optimizing item combinations per shipment reduces per-order costs

categories.name: Over-boxing
ideas: Manufacturer's packaging of some items is not durable for cargo shipping and must be placed in an additional outer box
Over-boxing increases package dimensions and volumetric weight, triggering higher carrier charges
Limited box assortment (8 sizes) forces use of larger boxes than needed for many items

categories.name: Box assortment
ideas: Too few box sizes means items are frequently shipped in oversized cartons
A carton-size study could identify the optimal mix of box dimensions
Better matching of box size to item dimensions reduces dimensional weight billing

categories.name: Distribution network
ideas: Single distribution center in Groveport, OH means all packages travel longer distances on average
East/west coast DCs would reduce average zone distance and lower carrier charges
Zone 7-8 shipments from a single OH DC are far more expensive than zone 1-3

categories.name: Vendor contract
ideas: Single carrier vendor limits negotiating leverage
Renegotiating volume discounts or adding a second carrier could reduce per-unit costs
Benchmarking vendor rates against market rates to identify savings opportunity

recommendation: Short-term: raise S&H prices on Expedited shipments (Lower 48 and AK&HI), Ground shipments to AK&HI, and the 44 identified fixed-price SKUs — this addresses ~30% of current losses while putting only ~11% of merchandise business at risk
Do not raise Ground Lower 48 prices as this represents ~91% of business and price increases risk demand reduction for the core business
risks: Raising prices may put the client at a competitive disadvantage relative to peers who are currently at price parity
Even a small drop in demand from AK&HI or Expedited customers could offset the margin improvement
Fixed-price SKU customers may shift purchasing behavior if those 44 items see price increases
next_steps: Conduct a 'carton-size study' to determine optimal assortment of shipping box dimensions — this is the primary long-term cost reduction lever
Explore expanding the distribution network with east coast and west coast fulfillment centers to reduce average carrier zone distance
Renegotiate carrier contract leveraging volume; consider dual-carrier strategy to improve rate benchmarking
Analyze demand patterns for the 44 high-loss fixed-price SKUs to determine whether repricing or discontinuation is optimal
